gemini_translation: You don't wear shoes in thorns and you are running; do you have the strength of a cow?
gemini_interpretation: It is foolish to engage in a difficult or dangerous task without proper preparation or protection, as it suggests an unrealistic overestimation of one's own capabilities.
mistral_translation: You do not wear shoes while the thorn is running; do you have the strength of a cow?
mistral_interpretation: It is foolish to ignore obvious dangers or fail to prepare adequately for challenges.
llama_translation: He doesn't wear shoes inside the masquerade's house, yet he's boasting of strength
llama_interpretation: One should not boast of abilities they have not demonstrated in a challenging situation.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Okotorobo-ó yé ẹyin sílẹ̀, àdàbà ńgarùn wo ẹyin ẹlẹ́yin.
english_literal: Okotorobo the bird lays an egg, and the turtle dove stretches its neck to inspect the egg that does not belong to it.
interpretation_gold: One should mind one's own business.
deepseek_translation: The hawk abandons the eggs, the dove comes to inspect the eggs of the hen.
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb warns against neglecting one's responsibilities, as others may take advantage of the situation.
claude_translation: The okotorobo bird has laid eggs on the ground, the dove is looking longingly at another's eggs.
claude_interpretation: People often desire what others have while neglecting or undervaluing their own possessions.
gemini_translation: The Okotorobo bird lays its eggs on the ground, the dove watches the eggs of the egg-layer.
gemini_interpretation: This proverb highlights the irony of someone neglecting their own responsibilities while being overly concerned with or observing the affairs of others.
mistral_translation: The one-legged person does not abandon eggs, the dove is counting the eggs of the egg-seller
mistral_interpretation: Do not neglect your responsibilities or possessions, as others may be monitoring or waiting to take advantage of your negligence.
llama_translation: The tortoise's mother is on the ground, the lizard's mother is on the wall.
llama_interpretation: This proverb highlights the differences in people's circumstances and backgrounds.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: O fi awọ ẹkùn ṣẹbọ àìkú; ẹkùn ìbá má kùú ìwọ ìbá rawọ ẹ̀ ṣoògùn?
english_literal: You use a leopard's skin as an ingredient for medicine to hold off death; had the leopard not died would you have had access to its hide for the medicine?
interpretation_gold: One should not chase impossible dreams.
deepseek_translation: He used the skin of a leopard for sacrifice to avoid death; if the leopard were alive, would you dare rub its body for medicine?
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb warns against taking advantage of someone's weakness or absence, as they would not dare to do so if the person were present or strong.
claude_translation: He used leopard's skin to make medicine against death; if leopards don't die, would you buy their skin for medicine?
claude_interpretation: It is illogical to trust something that contradicts itself or to believe in solutions that don't work for their own source.
gemini_translation: You used the skin of a leopard to make a charm for immortality; if the leopard had not died, would you have been able to use its skin for medicine?
gemini_interpretation: One cannot achieve a desired outcome without the necessary sacrifice or prerequisite event, even if that event is undesirable.
mistral_translation: You use a leopard's skin to offer sacrifice for immortality; if the leopard had not died, would you have gotten its skin to use as medicine?
mistral_interpretation: One cannot achieve great things without the sacrifices or contributions of others.
llama_translation: He used the leopard's skin to deceive the death; will the leopard's skin not be torn when it sees the hunter?
llama_interpretation: One's deceitful actions will eventually be exposed when faced with the consequences.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Ogún mbókòó? Òwe aṣiwèrè.
english_literal: Twenty or a score? An imbecile's puzzle.
interpretation_gold: Trust an imbecile to pose stupid questions.
deepseek_translation: Twenty is a hoe? A proverb of madness.
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb criticizes nonsensical or illogical statements, implying they are as absurd as calling a number a farming tool.
claude_translation: Is Ogun carrying a hoe? It's the proverb of a mad person.
claude_interpretation: It is foolish to question whether the god of iron and farming would carry the very tool he represents and governs.
gemini_translation: Is war coming? A proverb of a madman.
gemini_interpretation: It is foolish to anticipate or provoke conflict unnecessarily.
mistral_translation: Twenty heads? A proverb of a madman.
mistral_interpretation: It mocks someone who overcomplicates a simple matter, like a fool trying to count too many things at once.
llama_translation: Ogún is not a farmer? It is a proverb.
llama_interpretation: This proverb highlights the importance of knowing one's limits and not pretending to be something one is not.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Ojú tó rọ̀ nirorẹ́ ńsọ.
english_literal: Pimples attack only faces that are delicate.
interpretation_gold: People always take advantage of gentle people.
deepseek_translation: The eye that sees the farm is watering it.
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb teaches that seeing potential or opportunity is the first step toward nurturing and achieving success.
claude_translation: The eye that sheds tears is the one that speaks kindness
claude_interpretation: Those who have experienced suffering or hardship are often the most compassionate and understanding toward others.
gemini_translation: The eye that cries is the one that tells the story.
gemini_interpretation: Those who have experienced hardship are best positioned to recount its details and impact.
gemini_raw: {"translation": "The eye that cries is the one that tells the story.", "interpretation": "Those who have experienced hardship are best positioned to recount its details and impact."}
mistral_translation: The eye that cries will eventually dry up and heal.
mistral_interpretation: Sorrow or hardship is temporary, and one will eventually recover from it.
llama_translation: The eye that sees tomorrow is the one that is awake
llama_interpretation: Vigilance and preparedness are necessary for a successful future.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Orín yí, ìlù-ú yí padà.
english_literal: The song changes, and the drumming changes to suit.
interpretation_gold: One should match one's behavior to one's circumstances.
deepseek_translation: The song changes, the drum changes.
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb signifies that situations and circumstances are constantly evolving, requiring adaptability.
claude_translation: This song, this drum has changed.
claude_interpretation: The situation or circumstances have completely changed from what they used to be.
gemini_translation: The song changes, the drum changes.
gemini_interpretation: Circumstances dictate a change in approach or response.
gemini_raw: {"translation": "The song changes, the drum changes.", "interpretation": "Circumstances dictate a change in approach or response."}
mistral_translation: This song, this drumming has returned.
mistral_interpretation: A situation or event that was thought to be over has unexpectedly repeated itself.
llama_translation: This song, the drumming of it is enough
llama_interpretation: One's actions or behavior can be sufficient to reveal one's true nature or intentions.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: “Ó ṣe mí rí”; ògbó adìẹ-ẹ́ rí àwòdì sá.
english_literal: “I have experienced it before”; a grown chicken flees at the sight of a kite.
interpretation_gold: One learns to run from danger once one has recognized it for what it is.
deepseek_translation: “It happened to me”; the old man saw the hawk and ran.
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb warns that past experiences should teach caution, as the old man fled upon seeing the hawk due to prior harm.
claude_translation: It has done me harm; the hen's elder saw the hawk and ran away
claude_interpretation: Experience teaches wisdom - those who have faced danger before know to avoid it when they see it coming again.
gemini_translation: “It happened to me”; the old hen saw the hawk and ran away.
gemini_interpretation: Experience teaches wisdom, as even an old hen, having encountered danger before, knows to flee from a hawk.
gemini_raw: {"translation": "“It happened to me”; the old hen saw the hawk and ran away.", "interpretation": "Experience teaches wisdom, as even an old hen, having encountered danger before, knows to flee from a hawk."}
mistral_translation: “You did it to me”; the old hen sees the hawk fleeing
mistral_interpretation: The proverb teaches that those with experience can recognize danger or deception even when others do not.
llama_translation: He did me a favour; the hen sees the hawk's shadow
llama_interpretation: One's enemies can see the danger that one cannot see.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Onígi ní ńfigi ẹ̀ dọ́pọ̀.
english_literal: It is the firewood seller who sets a low price for his wares.
interpretation_gold: People take their cue from the owner of a thing in placing a value on it.
deepseek_translation: The owner of the wood is the one who piles the wood.
deepseek_interpretation: Only the person in charge has the authority to make decisions or take action.
claude_translation: The owner of the stick is the one using his stick to stir the soup
claude_interpretation: Only the person who owns or controls something has the right to decide how it should be used.
gemini_translation: The owner of the wood uses his wood to make a replacement.
gemini_interpretation: People are responsible for replacing what they have lost or used up.
gemini_raw: {"translation": "The owner of the wood uses his wood to make a replacement.", "interpretation": "People are responsible for replacing what they have lost or used up."}
mistral_translation: It is the owner of the log that is cutting it to size for the mortar.
mistral_interpretation: One should take responsibility for their own problems and not expect others to solve them.
llama_translation: The wall is leaning on the fence.
llama_interpretation: One who is weak or vulnerable often relies on someone or something stronger for support.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Okotorobo-ó tùyẹ́ sílẹ̀ ọmọ titún ńgbe jó; ó ní ó rọ òun lọ́rùn lòún tu ú?
english_literal: Okotorobo, a bird, casts away a feather, and a young chick picks it up to dance with it; the one who shed the feathers asks, would I have discarded it if it was not a nuisance.
interpretation_gold: One should be careful before taking over things that others have rejected.
deepseek_translation: The old grasshopper jumps aside for the new grasshopper to dance; does it say it is lighter than it?
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb teaches humility and respect for elders, emphasizing that stepping aside for the younger generation does not diminish one's worth.
claude_translation: The okotorobo bird drops its feathers to the ground and a new chick picks them up to dance; it asks 'did it grow these feathers on its own neck before plucking them?'
claude_interpretation: People should not take credit for or boast about things they did not create or earn themselves.
gemini_translation: The Okotorobo bird defecated on the ground, and the newborn child picked it up to play; it said, 'Did it make my neck comfortable that I should pick it up?'
gemini_interpretation: This proverb highlights the innocence and lack of discernment in children, who may engage with things without understanding their true nature or implications.
mistral_translation: The hunchback spreads a mat for the newborn to dance on; he asks if it is easy for him to spread it?
mistral_interpretation: The proverb criticizes those who create difficulties for others yet complain about the effort it takes to do so.
llama_translation: The tortoise that has a child on its back is dancing; it says it is the child that is dancing on its back
llama_interpretation: This proverb highlights the tendency for people to shift blame or responsibility to others, often to avoid accountability.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Owú pani ju kùm̀mọ̀.
english_literal: Jealousy kills more surely than a cudgel.
interpretation_gold: Jealousy is a dangerous thing.
deepseek_translation: Hunger kills more than poison.
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb emphasizes that the suffering caused by hunger is more severe and deadly than that caused by poison.
claude_translation: Cotton kills more than a club.
claude_interpretation: Soft, gentle things can be more dangerous or harmful than obviously threatening ones.
gemini_translation: Jealousy kills more than a club.
gemini_interpretation: Jealousy is a destructive emotion that can cause more harm than physical violence.
mistral_translation: Cotton kills more than a knife.
mistral_interpretation: Seemingly harmless things can cause greater harm than obvious dangers.
llama_translation: A dead person is better than a mute person.
llama_interpretation: It is better to be gone than to be present but unable to express oneself or contribute to a situation.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Olóhun kì í rí ohun ẹ̀ kó pè é lórò.
english_literal: The owner will not see what he owns and call it a fearful; abomination.
interpretation_gold: One cannot be fearful of what one owns.
deepseek_translation: God does not see something and call it a mystery.
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb means that nothing is beyond God's understanding or control.
claude_translation: God does not see something and call it expensive.
claude_interpretation: Nothing is too costly or difficult for God to provide or accomplish.
gemini_translation: The owner does not see his property and call it a taboo.
gemini_interpretation: People do not speak ill of or condemn what belongs to them or what they value.
mistral_translation: God does not see a thing and delay in punishing it as wrongdoing
mistral_interpretation: Divine justice is certain and will not be delayed for any wrongdoing
llama_translation: The deaf does not hear the thing that is called by its name
llama_interpretation: One who is unwilling to listen or pay attention will not understand or respond to a message, no matter how clearly it is communicated.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Olóhun-ún dolè; “Gbà bù jẹ́” dolóhun.
english_literal: The owner becomes a thief; “Take this and eat” becomes the owner.
interpretation_gold: The tables are turned, such that the rightful owner is displaced by a usurper.
deepseek_translation: God owns the house; 'Accept and endure' owns God.
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb teaches that patience and endurance are divine virtues favored by God.
claude_translation: The creditor becomes the debtor; 'Take and eat' becomes the creditor.
claude_interpretation: Roles and circumstances can reverse unexpectedly, where the one who was owed becomes the one who owes.
gemini_translation: The owner became lazy; 'Take and eat' became the owner.
gemini_interpretation: Negligence and inaction can lead to the loss of one's possessions or authority to those who are more proactive.
mistral_translation: God owns the house; 'Please, let me have it' owns God.
mistral_interpretation: The proverb highlights the power of polite and humble requests in overcoming even divine authority.
llama_translation: The one who has a secret is at home; 'Take and eat' is the secret.
llama_interpretation: This proverb cautions against revealing confidential information, as it can lead to trouble.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Orí ọ̀kẹ́rẹ́ popo láwo; bí a wí fọ́mọ ẹni a gbọ́ràn.
english_literal: The squirrel's head sits in a plate like a lump; if one counsels one's child it should listen.
interpretation_gold: Refusal to listen to counsel leads to disaster.
deepseek_translation: The head of the stranger is big like a pot; if we mention our child's name, we listen.
deepseek_interpretation: People often pay more attention to outsiders than their own family members.
claude_translation: The head of a squirrel is completely bald; when one speaks to one's child, one listens to advice.
claude_interpretation: Just as a squirrel's bald head is obvious to all, when you counsel your child, you should also be open to receiving wisdom in return.
gemini_translation: The head of the distant one is bald; if we speak to our child, they will obey.
gemini_interpretation: This proverb suggests that while outsiders may be difficult to influence, one's own children are expected to be receptive to guidance and instruction.
gemini_raw: {"translation": "The head of the distant one is bald; if we speak to our child, they will obey.", "interpretation": "This proverb suggests that while outsiders may be difficult to influence, one's own children are expected to be receptive to guidance and instruction."}
mistral_translation: The head of a squirrel is full of lines like a woven mat; if we speak in parables, our children will understand advice
mistral_interpretation: Using simple, relatable examples makes wisdom easier to grasp and remember for future generations
llama_translation: The head of the okere tree is big on the outside; when you peel it, you will see the smallness of its content.
llama_interpretation: Appearance can be deceiving, and true worth is often hidden beneath the surface.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Ojú kì í pọ́nni ká mu ìṣápá; òùngbẹ kì í gbẹni ká mu ẹ̀jẹ̀.
english_literal: One is never so desperate that one drinks red sorrel juice; one is never so thirsty that one drinks blood.
interpretation_gold: Desperation must never push one beyond the bounds of acceptable behavior.
deepseek_translation: The eye does not hurt someone and then make them take a staff; the mouth does not offend someone and then make them take a knife.
deepseek_interpretation: One's actions or words should not provoke others to retaliate with violence.
claude_translation: Eyes do not deceive one to drink palm wine; thirst does not dry one up to drink blood
claude_interpretation: One should not use circumstances as an excuse to engage in forbidden or harmful actions.
gemini_translation: The eye does not become red (inflamed) and one drinks sorrel; one does not become thirsty and drink blood.
gemini_interpretation: One should not resort to inappropriate or harmful solutions when faced with a problem.
mistral_translation: The eye does not become swollen so that we can drink bean soup; the throat does not become hoarse so that we can drink blood
mistral_interpretation: People do not endure suffering or hardship just to satisfy the desires or whims of others
llama_translation: The eye does not go to sleep and the eyelid does; the ear does not go to sleep and the earring does.
llama_interpretation: One part of a whole cannot function independently without the other.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Oòrùn kì í jẹ iṣu àgbà kó má mọbẹ̀.
english_literal: An elder does not lose his yams to the sun without knowing where the event happened.
interpretation_gold: A grown up person should know where he went wrong and make amends accordingly.
deepseek_translation: The sun does not eat an old yam without knowing its place.
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb means that experience and wisdom come with age, and elders should be respected for their knowledge.
claude_translation: The sun does not eat an elder's yam without knowing how to peel it
claude_interpretation: One should not attempt tasks or claim privileges without having the necessary knowledge, skills, or wisdom to handle them properly.
gemini_translation: The sun does not burn an elder's yam without it knowing the soup.
gemini_interpretation: An elder's experience and wisdom allow them to anticipate and prepare for challenges.
gemini_raw: {"translation": "The sun does not burn an elder's yam without it knowing the soup.", "interpretation": "An elder's experience and wisdom allow them to anticipate and prepare for challenges."}
mistral_translation: The sun does not eat an elder's yam without adding salt to it
mistral_interpretation: Respect for elders ensures their wisdom and contributions are properly valued and preserved
llama_translation: The sky does not eat the yam of the elder and then forget
llama_interpretation: One should not forget the favors or kindness received from elders or those in positions of authority.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Òjòwú ò lẹ́ran láyà.
english_literal: The jealous woman lacks flesh on her chest.
interpretation_gold: Excessive jealousy eats up the jealous.
deepseek_translation: The rain does not listen to the goat.
deepseek_interpretation: Nature's forces do not heed the complaints or desires of individuals.
claude_translation: The coward has no courage in his heart.
claude_interpretation: A person who lacks bravery cannot find inner strength when faced with challenges.
gemini_translation: A jealous person has no meat in their chest.
gemini_interpretation: Jealousy is a destructive emotion that consumes the jealous person from within, leaving them with nothing of value.
gemini_raw: {"translation": "A jealous person has no meat in their chest.", "interpretation": "Jealousy is a destructive emotion that consumes the jealous person from within, leaving them with nothing of value."}
mistral_translation: A jealous rain does not wet the meat in the open.
mistral_interpretation: Jealousy or ill-will from others cannot harm you if you are honest and transparent in your actions.
llama_translation: The rain does not wet the inside of the belly
llama_interpretation: One's problems or troubles are not always visible to others.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: O ní kí ará ọ̀run ṣe oore fún ọ; bẹ́ẹ̀ni o rí ẹni tí eégún ńlé, tó fá lọ́bẹ̀ lá.
english_literal: You pray to the being from heaven to grant you a boon; yet you can see the person being chased by the masquerader and whose stew the masquerader has consumed.
interpretation_gold: One should not expect to receive better treatment from a person who is known to be vicious to others.
deepseek_translation: He said the people of heaven should do you good; did you see the person the masquerade is chasing, that he took to the farm?
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb warns against relying on divine intervention without taking practical action to address one's problems.
claude_translation: He says the heavenly beings should do you a favor; likewise you see someone being chased by masquerades who draws a knife to cut through.
claude_interpretation: When seeking divine intervention or help, one must also be prepared to take decisive action to solve their own problems.
gemini_translation: He says that the people of heaven should do good for you; yet you see someone being chased by a masquerade, and he is licking soup.
gemini_interpretation: This proverb highlights the irony and foolishness of seeking blessings from distant sources while ignoring immediate dangers or opportunities.
gemini_raw: {"translation": "He says that the people of heaven should do good for you; yet you see someone being chased by a masquerade, and he is licking soup.", "interpretation": "This proverb highlights the irony and foolishness of seeking blessings from distant sources while ignoring immediate dangers or opportunities."}
mistral_translation: He said the heavenly beings should do you a favor; meanwhile, you see the person the masquerade is visiting, who has taken away the knife.
mistral_interpretation: Do not ignore immediate help from those around you while waiting for distant or unlikely assistance.
llama_translation: He said the people of heaven should make a road for him; but when he got there, he saw someone whose load was heavier, and he was carrying it on his head.
llama_interpretation: One's problems are relative and may be less burdensome compared to others.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Olówó á wá; aláwìn á wá; ìlú tí à ńgbé la gbé ńgbàwìn; à-rà-àì-san ni ò súnwọ̀n.
english_literal: Those who have money will come, and those who will buy on credit will come; it is in one's town that one buys on credit; failure to eventually pay up is what is bad.
interpretation_gold: There is nothing bad about buying on credit, as long as one eventually pays.
deepseek_translation: The wealthy will come; the poor will come; the town we live in we live in poverty; owing debts is not good.
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb warns against living beyond one's means and the consequences of accumulating debt.
claude_translation: The wealthy will come; the indebted will come; it is in the town where we live that we seek credit; buying without paying is not proper.
claude_interpretation: It is acceptable to seek credit within your own community, but one must always honor their debts and pay what is owed.
gemini_translation: The rich will come; the debtor will come; it is in the town where we live that we borrow; it is not paying back that is bad.
gemini_interpretation: Borrowing is a natural part of community life, but failing to repay debts is unacceptable.
gemini_raw: {"translation": "The rich will come; the debtor will come; it is in the town where we live that we borrow; it is not paying back that is bad.", "interpretation": "Borrowing is a natural part of community life, but failing to repay debts is unacceptable."}
mistral_translation: The rich will come; the poor will come; the town we live in is where we spend our time; the one who buys on credit does not sleep soundly.
mistral_interpretation: Regardless of wealth or status, everyone faces their own struggles, and debt brings constant worry.
llama_translation: Money is coming; beauty is coming; the town where we live is the one we will take to heaven; it is the one we will not leave behind.
llama_interpretation: One's community and heritage are more valuable than material wealth or physical appearance.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Òwú kì í là kínú bí olóko.
english_literal: The cotton seed does not open and thus anger the farmer.
interpretation_gold: The success of one's venture does not make one angry.
deepseek_translation: Cotton does not tear in the mouth like cornmeal.
deepseek_interpretation: Different things require different approaches or treatments.
claude_translation: Cotton does not spread out in the farm like the farmer.
claude_interpretation: A person should not overstep their boundaries or act beyond their proper role and status.
gemini_translation: Cotton does not burst open in the heart like the farmer.
gemini_interpretation: The proverb highlights that while a farmer's heart may be burdened with worries about their crops, the cotton itself does not share or express such anxieties.
gemini_raw: {"translation": "Cotton does not burst open in the heart like the farmer.", "interpretation": "The proverb highlights that while a farmer's heart may be burdened with worries about their crops, the cotton itself does not share or express such anxieties."}
mistral_translation: Cotton does not tear inside like the farmer's wife
mistral_interpretation: Outsiders should not interfere in a household's internal conflicts or private matters.
llama_translation: The death of a slave does not affect the farmer
llama_interpretation: The loss of a subordinate or someone of lower status does not significantly impact the person of higher status or authority.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: “Ó ḿbọ̀, ó ḿbọ̀!” la fi ńdẹ́rù ba ọmọdé; bó bá dé tán ẹ̀rù a tán.
english_literal: “It's coming! It's coming!” is what one says to frighten a child; after it has arrived it loses all its terror.
interpretation_gold: Looming problems often cause consternation out of all proportion to their real damaging force.
deepseek_translation: “It is heavy, it is heavy!” is how we carry a child; when it is time to put down, we put down.
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb teaches that responsibilities, though burdensome, are temporary and should be handled with care until they are no longer needed.
claude_translation: It's coming, it's coming! is what we use to frighten children; when it arrives completely, the fear disappears.
claude_interpretation: Empty threats lose their power once people realize there are no real consequences behind them.
gemini_translation: “It’s coming, it’s coming!” is how we scare a child; when it has arrived, the fear ends.
gemini_interpretation: Anticipation of a threat can be more frightening than the actual event, which often proves less daunting than imagined.
mistral_translation: “It is coming, it is coming!” is how we use to deceive a child; when it finally arrives, the load is gone.
mistral_interpretation: The proverb warns against empty promises or false assurances that lead to disappointment when expectations are not met.
llama_translation: “It is a lion, it is a lion!” is what is used to deceive a child; when it gets there, it is just a goat.
llama_interpretation: This proverb warns against exaggeration or false pretenses, which can lead to disappointment or disillusionment.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Ohun tí kò jẹ́ káṣọ pé méjì ni ò jẹ́ kó dú.
english_literal: The same thing that keeps one from having more than one item of clothing also keeps that one from blackening from dirt.
interpretation_gold: Misfortune teaches one fortitude; scarcity teaches one to be thrifty.
deepseek_translation: What does not allow the cloth to be two does not allow it to be torn.
deepseek_interpretation: Unity and togetherness prevent destruction and conflict.
claude_translation: What does not allow one to count two does not allow one to count three
claude_interpretation: If you cannot handle small responsibilities or tasks, you cannot handle bigger ones.
gemini_translation: What prevents a cloth from being two is what prevents it from being black.
gemini_interpretation: A single, underlying cause often explains multiple related problems or deficiencies.
mistral_translation: What is not enough to make two garments is not enough to make even one
mistral_interpretation: If resources are insufficient for a complete or proper task, it is better not to attempt it at all
llama_translation: What does not eat two things is what we eat to be satisfied
llama_interpretation: Moderation is key to satisfaction and contentment.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: “Òkè ìhín ò jẹ́ ká rí tọ̀ún” ò ṣéé pa lówe nílé àna ẹni.
english_literal: “The nearer hill kept one from seeing the farther one” is not a proverb one uses in one's parents-in-law's home.
interpretation_gold: There are some obligations one cannot sidestep with flippant excuses.
deepseek_translation: The hill of ants does not allow one to see the valley.
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb warns that focusing too much on minor issues can prevent one from seeing the bigger picture or more important matters.
claude_translation: The hill over there that prevents us from seeing beyond cannot be killed with proverbs in one's in-laws' house
claude_interpretation: Some problems or obstacles cannot be solved through indirect speech or diplomacy, especially when you're in a delicate social position where you must be careful with your words.
gemini_translation: “The hill here prevents us from seeing the one over there” cannot be used as a proverb in one's in-laws' house.
gemini_interpretation: One should be careful about what they say in the presence of their in-laws, as certain statements might be misinterpreted or cause offense.
mistral_translation: The hill behind does not prevent us from seeing the one in front; it should not be used as a proverb in one's own hometown
mistral_interpretation: One should not use familiar or local knowledge to boast or deceive those who already know the truth.
llama_translation: The hill of yam heaps does not prevent one from seeing the road to the farm of another person
llama_interpretation: One's own success or abundance should not blind them to the struggles or needs of others.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Orí tó kọ ẹrù, owó ní ńnáni.
english_literal: A head that refuses “to carry” loads will cost its owner some money.
interpretation_gold: It costs money to get others to do for one what one refuses to do for oneself.
deepseek_translation: The head that refuses to carry a load, money is what it will carry.
deepseek_interpretation: If you avoid responsibilities, you will face financial struggles.
claude_translation: The head that refuses to carry load, money is what burns it.
claude_interpretation: Those who avoid hard work will find themselves spending money unnecessarily or suffering financial consequences.
gemini_translation: The head that carries a load is the one that earns money.
gemini_interpretation: Hard work and effort are necessary to achieve success and gain rewards.
mistral_translation: A head that carries a load, money is what it seeks
mistral_interpretation: One who bears responsibility naturally looks for financial reward or support to sustain their efforts.
llama_translation: The head that wears the cap of a slave, money is its owner
llama_interpretation: Wealth and material possessions can enslave and control an individual.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Ó ti ojú orun wá ó ńfọ ẹnà; ó ní “ẹ jẹ́ ká máa ji ní mẹ́mu-mẹ́mu.”
english_literal: He woke up from sleep and spoke in scrambled language; he said, “Let us wake it in moos.”
interpretation_gold: An ignorant person will always make stupid suggestions.
deepseek_translation: He came from the sky and was blowing the trumpet; he said, "Let us wake up gradually."
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb advises taking things slowly and carefully rather than rushing into actions.
claude_translation: He came from the face of heaven and is washing his hands; he says 'let us wake up gently-gently.'
claude_interpretation: Someone who has experienced divine favor or good fortune should approach life with humility and gentleness rather than arrogance.
gemini_translation: He came from the land of dreams and is clearing the path; he says, 'Let's be stealing little by little.'
gemini_interpretation: This proverb describes someone who, having just woken up and still disoriented, proposes a foolish or impractical idea, highlighting the absurdity of acting without full awareness or consideration.
mistral_translation: The one who came from the sky is boasting about the path; he says, 'Let us wake up gently.'
mistral_interpretation: A person who benefits from external help or privilege should not boast or act arrogantly, as their success is not solely their own effort.
llama_translation: He came from heaven and was crying; he said 'let us eat and be satisfied in abundance'.
llama_interpretation: This proverb teaches that one should appreciate and be content with the blessings they have.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Orin tí ò ṣoro-ó dá kì í ṣòro-ó gbè; bí ó bá ní “héééé,” à ní “háááá.”
english_literal: A song that is not difficult to lead is not difficult to follow; if the leader sings “haaaay,” one responds “haaaah.”
interpretation_gold: One expends on a task only the amount of effort commensurate with it.
deepseek_translation: A song that is not difficult to sing is not difficult to carry; if it says 'héééé,' we say 'háááá.'
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb emphasizes that tasks which appear easy require little effort or thought to accomplish.
claude_translation: A song that is not difficult to start is not difficult to carry; if it has 'héééé,' we respond with 'háááá.'
claude_interpretation: Things that are easy to begin are usually easy to continue, and participation becomes natural when you understand the pattern.
gemini_translation: A song that is not difficult to compose is not difficult to sing; if it says “heeee,” we say “haaaa.”
gemini_interpretation: Simple tasks or situations are easy to respond to and manage.
mistral_translation: A song that is not difficult to sing does not become difficult to sing; if it has 'heee,' it will have 'haaaa.'
mistral_interpretation: A task that appears simple at first will reveal its true challenges as you attempt it.
llama_translation: A song that does not make you dance will not make you dance; if it says 'héééé,' you will say 'háááá.'
llama_interpretation: This proverb highlights the idea that people tend to respond in kind to the energy or attitude they receive.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: O sá fún ikú, o bọ́ sí àkọ̀ idà.
english_literal: You run from death and seek refuge in a scabbard.
interpretation_gold: Said of a person who has got himself/herself in a worse predicament from the one he/she was fleeing from.
deepseek_translation: He ran from death, but ran into the sheath of the sword.
deepseek_interpretation: Avoiding one danger only to encounter a worse one.
claude_translation: He ran from death and fell into a sword's sheath
claude_interpretation: Trying to escape one danger often leads to encountering an even greater one.
gemini_translation: He ran from death, he fell into a sword sheath.
gemini_interpretation: Attempting to escape one danger can lead one directly into another, equally perilous situation.
gemini_raw: {"translation": "He ran from death, he fell into a sword sheath.", "interpretation": "Attempting to escape one danger can lead one directly into another, equally perilous situation."}
mistral_translation: You ran from death, you stumbled into the sheath of a sword
mistral_interpretation: Avoiding one danger may lead you into an even greater one
llama_translation: He made a sacrifice for death, and it reached the left side of the sword.
llama_interpretation: One's actions can have unintended and far-reaching consequences.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Onígẹ̀gẹ́ fìlẹ̀kẹ̀ dọ́pọ̀; adámú fi sàárà san ẹgbẹ̀ta.
english_literal: The goitered person sets a low price on beads; the person with a blocked nose repays six thousand cowries with alms.
interpretation_gold: One usually sets little value on what one cannot use.
deepseek_translation: The bald-headed one wears a wig; the hairy one shaves his head.
deepseek_interpretation: People often desire what they do not have while neglecting what they possess.
claude_translation: The banana seller exchanges banana for coins; the groundnut seller uses small change to pay for thirty kobo worth.
claude_interpretation: Small consistent transactions and careful money management can accumulate into significant amounts over time.
gemini_translation: The one who wears beads uses them to replace a debt; the one who wears a cap uses it to pay six hundred cowries.
gemini_interpretation: This proverb highlights the resourcefulness and adaptability of individuals in using available assets to resolve financial obligations, even if unconventional.
mistral_translation: The lazy person strings beads to sell; the restless one pays double the price for a gourd.
mistral_interpretation: The proverb highlights how laziness and impatience both lead to unnecessary waste or loss.
llama_translation: The tortoise's shell is not complete; Adamu uses a rag to cover his buttocks.
llama_interpretation: One uses available resources to cover up one's shortcomings or inadequacies.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Ogún kì í pọ̀ ká pín fún aládùúgbò.
english_literal: The inheritance is never so abundant that one shares it with neighbors.
interpretation_gold: However abundantly one is blessed one should manage one's resources wisely.
deepseek_translation: Twenty is not too many to share with a neighbor.
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb emphasizes the importance of generosity and community support, suggesting that no amount is too large to share with those around you.
claude_translation: Twenty cannot be many enough to share with neighbors
claude_interpretation: No matter how much you have, it's never enough to satisfy everyone who expects to benefit from your resources.
gemini_translation: War does not become so much that it is shared with a neighbor.
gemini_interpretation: One's personal troubles or burdens are not meant to be shared or distributed among others, especially those not directly involved.
mistral_translation: Twenty does not gather together to be shared with a neighbor.
mistral_interpretation: People should not expect others to share their resources when they have enough for themselves.
llama_translation: War does not allow one to choose a companion
llama_interpretation: In times of crisis, one may have to accept help from anyone, regardless of their character or background.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Olóògùn ní ńṣe bí a-láigbọ́-mọ̀ràn; bí ogun ó bàá wọ̀lú ọlọgbọ́n là ńfọ̀rọ̀ lọ̀.
english_literal: The medicine man behaves like a person impervious to wise counsel; if war threatens a town the person to consult for counsel is the sage.
interpretation_gold: Trust rather in wisdom than in magical charms.
deepseek_translation: The medicine man behaves like one who lacks wisdom; when war comes to town, the wise man is the one who runs.
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb warns against underestimating the wise, as they know when to act or retreat for survival.
claude_translation: The medicine man acts like one who doesn't listen to advice; when war enters the town, it is to the wise person we run for counsel.
claude_interpretation: Those who ignore good advice in peaceful times will be sought after for wisdom when crisis strikes.
gemini_translation: The herbalist acts like one who does not know; if war is to enter the town, it is with the wise that one consults.
gemini_interpretation: Even experts may feign ignorance to gather information, and in times of crisis, it is crucial to seek counsel from the truly knowledgeable.
mistral_translation: The medicine owner acts as if he is ignorant; when war enters a wise person's town, we seek refuge with him.
mistral_interpretation: True wisdom or expertise is often hidden until the moment of need, when it becomes indispensable.
llama_translation: The herbalist treats as one who has not seen the forest; if the medicine does not kill the herbalist, it is the one he will use to treat others.
llama_interpretation: A person who has not experienced a situation firsthand may not fully understand its challenges.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Olé tó jí kàkàkí, níbo ni yó ti fọn ọ́n?
english_literal: A thief who stole a bugle, where will he blow it?
interpretation_gold: One should not waste one's efforts chasing something one can never use.
deepseek_translation: The thief who wakes the trumpeter, where will he blow the trumpet?
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb warns that actions meant to expose others may ultimately reveal one's own misdeeds.
claude_translation: A thief who steals a trumpet, where will he blow it?
claude_interpretation: Some stolen goods are too conspicuous or distinctive to use without revealing the theft.
gemini_translation: A thief who stole a trumpet, where will he blow it?
gemini_interpretation: One should consider the consequences and practicality of their actions, especially when those actions are illicit or inappropriate.
mistral_translation: The thief who wakes up to the sound of a trumpet, where will he have hidden his loot?
mistral_interpretation: A person who acts recklessly or arrogantly will eventually expose their own wrongdoing.
llama_translation: A thief who steals a hen, where has he hidden it?
llama_interpretation: This proverb teaches that every action has consequences and one's misdeeds will eventually be exposed.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Odó iyán ò jẹ́ gún ẹ̀lú; odó ẹ̀lú ò jẹ́ gúnyán; àtẹ tá-a fi ńpàtẹ ìlẹ̀kẹ̀, a ò jẹ́ fi pàtẹ ọ̀rúnlá.
english_literal: The mortar used for pounding yams will not do for pounding indigo leaves; the mortar for pounding indigo leaves will not do for yams; the tray on which beads are displayed for sale will not do for displaying dried okro.
interpretation_gold: Each object has its proper uses.
deepseek_translation: The mortar for pounding yam cannot be used to pound ẹ̀lú; the mortar for pounding ẹ̀lú cannot be used to pound yam; the grinding stone used for grinding beads cannot be used to grind ọ̀rúnlá.
deepseek_interpretation: Each tool has its specific purpose and should not be misused for tasks it wasn't designed for.
claude_translation: The mortar for pounding yam is not suitable for pounding elu; the mortar for elu is not suitable for pounding yam; the flat stone used for flattening beads cannot be used to flatten Orunmila.
claude_interpretation: Different tools are designed for specific purposes, and sacred things require appropriate reverence and cannot be treated with ordinary implements.
gemini_translation: The yam pounder cannot pound indigo; the indigo pounder cannot pound yam; the tray used for displaying beads, we cannot use it to display kola nuts.
gemini_interpretation: Each tool or person has a specific purpose or role, and it is inappropriate to use them for tasks they are not suited for.
gemini_raw: {"translation": "The yam pounder cannot pound indigo; the indigo pounder cannot pound yam; the tray used for displaying beads, we cannot use it to display kola nuts.", "interpretation": "Each tool or person has a specific purpose or role, and it is inappropriate to use them for tasks they are not suited for."}
mistral_translation: The mortar for pounding yam does not climb the hill; the mortar of the hill does not pound yam; the mat we use to string beads on the ground, we do not use to string the ọ̀rúnlá beads.
mistral_interpretation: Every tool or method has its proper context or use, and one should not force what is unsuitable for a particular situation.
llama_translation: The river of yam does not flow to the town; the river of the town does not flow to the yam; we use the river to wash the feet, we do not use it to wash the head.
llama_interpretation: One should prioritize and respect the proper order and hierarchy of things.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Òjòwú ò já gèlè; kooro ló lè já.
english_literal: The jealous woman does not snatch her head gear off; all she can do is threaten a fight.
interpretation_gold: Some people are all mouth and no action.
deepseek_translation: The scarf did not tear into a headtie; it tore into strips.
deepseek_interpretation: The outcome of a situation may not be as expected, but it still serves a purpose.
claude_translation: Jealousy cannot tear a headtie; only a sharp object can tear it.
claude_interpretation: Mere envy or ill-will cannot destroy something solid or well-established; only direct action or real force can cause damage.
gemini_translation: The jealous person does not tie a headtie; it is the bald person who can tie it.
gemini_interpretation: Those who are envious or critical of others often lack the ability or opportunity to achieve what they criticize.
mistral_translation: The rain does not remove the headtie; it is the wind that can remove it.
mistral_interpretation: External challenges alone cannot ruin one's dignity or status; it is one's own actions or carelessness that lead to downfall.
llama_translation: The rain does not beat the drum; it is the thunder that beats the drum.
llama_interpretation: Power and authority are not the same as the ability to take action or make things happen.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Ó ńti ilé bọ̀ kò ra ẹ̀gbẹ; ó dé oko tán ó ní ẹ̀gbẹ ni oníkú ẹ̀kọ.
english_literal: Leaving the home he did not purchase dried meat; after arriving on the farm he says dried meat is the indispensable thing to eat corn loaf with.
interpretation_gold: One should make provisions against one's future needs.
deepseek_translation: He who destroys his house does not buy a mat; he gets to the farm and says the mat belongs to the deceased farmer.
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb warns against destroying what you have, as you may later regret and falsely claim ownership of what remains.
claude_translation: He was coming from home and didn't buy palm wine; when he arrived at the farm he said palm wine is what the corn seller has.
claude_interpretation: People often make excuses or blame others for their own lack of preparation or foresight.
gemini_translation: He was coming from home and did not buy a side dish; when he got to the farm, he said the side dish is the owner of the eko (corn pudding).
gemini_interpretation: This proverb criticizes someone who is unprepared or lazy and then blames others or circumstances for their shortcomings.
gemini_raw: {"translation": "He was coming from home and did not buy a side dish; when he got to the farm, he said the side dish is the owner of the eko (corn pudding).", "interpretation": "This proverb criticizes someone who is unprepared or lazy and then blames others or circumstances for their shortcomings."}
mistral_translation: He was plastering the house and did not buy a fan; when he got to the farm, he said a fan is for the owner of the hoe
mistral_interpretation: People often neglect what they truly need until they are in a situation where it becomes essential.
llama_translation: He who doesn't learn at home doesn't learn in the farm; he gets to the farm and says learning is the death of a farmer.
llama_interpretation: One who fails to learn from their family and upbringing will struggle to learn and adapt in other environments.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Olóúnjẹ-ẹ́ tó-ó bá kú.
english_literal: Someone who has food is worth dying with.
interpretation_gold: Food is a good enough reason to cast one's lot with another person's.
deepseek_translation: The owner of food is the one who dies.
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb emphasizes that those who possess resources are often the ones who face the consequences or responsibilities.
claude_translation: The food owner who will die.
claude_interpretation: Everyone, regardless of their wealth or possessions, will eventually face death.
gemini_translation: The one who owns food will die.
gemini_interpretation: Even the wealthy and powerful are subject to mortality.
gemini_raw: {"translation": "The one who owns food will die.", "interpretation": "Even the wealthy and powerful are subject to mortality."}
mistral_translation: The owner of the food that is about to die.
mistral_interpretation: It warns against being overly possessive or greedy, as death can take everything away.
llama_translation: The one who eats alone will die alone
llama_interpretation: Selfishness and isolation can lead to one's downfall.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Onígbèsè tí ńpa àpatà ẹyẹ́lé.
english_literal: Habitual debtor who butchers a pigeon for sale.
interpretation_gold: The debtor is desperate, because there is not much to a pigeon, and few people eat pigeons anyway.
deepseek_translation: The hunter who kills pigeons with a club.
deepseek_interpretation: It criticizes unnecessary force or overkill in achieving a goal.
claude_translation: A debtor who is killing the dove's rock/stone
claude_interpretation: A person who destroys their own place of refuge or safety while trying to escape their problems will ultimately harm themselves.
gemini_translation: A debtor who kills a pigeon for sacrifice.
gemini_interpretation: It is foolish to incur more debt or waste resources when already in debt, as it exacerbates the problem.
mistral_translation: The debtor who kills a pigeon on a rock
mistral_interpretation: A person in debt should not live extravagantly or waste resources they do not truly possess.
llama_translation: The one who is lazy will be beaten by the ant.
llama_interpretation: Hard work and diligence are essential to avoid being surpassed by others.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Owó la fi ńlògbà; ọgbọ́n la fi ńgbélé ayé.
english_literal: It is with money that we secure pleasures; it is with wisdom that one secures a good life.
interpretation_gold: Riches are desirable, but wisdom is more valuable.
deepseek_translation: Money is used to grow old; wisdom is used to live on earth.
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb emphasizes that while money is necessary for survival, wisdom is essential for a meaningful life.
claude_translation: It is with money that we buy respect; it is with wisdom that we sustain life in the world.
claude_interpretation: While money can purchase temporary respect and status, it is wisdom that enables one to navigate and endure successfully in life.
gemini_translation: Money is used to cultivate a farm; wisdom is used to live life.
gemini_interpretation: While resources are essential for practical endeavors, wisdom is paramount for navigating the complexities of life successfully.
gemini_raw: {"translation": "Money is used to cultivate a farm; wisdom is used to live life.", "interpretation": "While resources are essential for practical endeavors, wisdom is paramount for navigating the complexities of life successfully."}
mistral_translation: We use money to build a fence; we use wisdom to navigate the world
mistral_interpretation: Wisdom is more valuable than wealth in overcoming life's challenges and earning respect
llama_translation: Money is used to take care of the body; wisdom is used to navigate the world.
llama_interpretation: Wisdom is more valuable than wealth in navigating life's challenges.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Ohun tí a ṣe nílé àna ẹni, “Ojú ńtì mí” kúrò níbẹ̀.
english_literal: What one does in the home of one's parents-in-law leaves no room for “I am bashful.”
interpretation_gold: One must not be reticent in doing whatever one must do.
deepseek_translation: What one does in the house of one's in-laws, 'My eyes are closed' is absent there.
deepseek_interpretation: This proverb warns that one's actions are always observed, even when one thinks they are unnoticed.
claude_translation: What one does in one's in-laws' house, 'I am ashamed' should be removed from there.
claude_interpretation: One should act confidently and without shame when visiting or living with in-laws, as hesitation or embarrassment can create awkwardness in family relationships.
gemini_translation: What is done in one's in-laws' house, "I am ashamed" is removed from there.
gemini_interpretation: One should not feel shame or embarrassment when performing duties or actions in their in-laws' home, as it is a place of acceptance and belonging.
mistral_translation: What one does in a neighbor's house, 'My eyes are closed' does not remain there
mistral_interpretation: Actions taken in secrecy or without accountability will eventually be exposed or have consequences.
llama_translation: What we do at home, 'my eyes are closed' will leave from there
llama_interpretation: One's secrets will eventually be exposed if they are not careful about their actions at home.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Owó ní ńpa ọjà ọ̀mọ̀ràn.
english_literal: It is money that brings a knowing person's trading to a conclusion.
interpretation_gold: A wise trader knows how to use his money to make his offer successful.
deepseek_translation: Money is what kills the wise person.
deepseek_interpretation: The proverb warns that greed or excessive pursuit of wealth can lead even the wisest to ruin.
claude_translation: Money is what kills the market of the wise person.
claude_interpretation: Even wise people can make poor decisions when money is involved, as financial considerations can cloud good judgment.
gemini_translation: Money kills the market of the wise.
gemini_interpretation: Even the most intelligent and skilled individuals can be hindered or rendered ineffective if they lack the necessary financial resources.
mistral_translation: Money is what kills the market of the wise child.
mistral_interpretation: Excessive wealth or greed can undermine the value of wisdom and good judgment.
llama_translation: Money is the one that kills the market of children
llama_interpretation: Wealth and material possessions can be a corrupting influence on the young.

part_theme: perspicaciousness, reasonableness, sagacity, savoir-faire, wisdom, worldly wisdom
yoruba: Ó di kan-nu-rin kan-nu-rin, agogo Ògúntólú.
english_literal: All one hears is noise without pattern, like that of Oguntolu's bell.
interpretation_gold: The statements being made are senseless.
deepseek_translation: It becomes step by step, the clock of Oguntolu.
